name: Riggs Bank

summary.text: Riggs Bank N.A. was a Washington, D.C. national bank whose embassy banking business included the Saudi Arabian embassy and Equatorial Guinea as its two largest embassy clients, and which held accounts for Chile's former ruler Augusto Pinochet. An OCC examination begun in January 2003 found tens of millions of dollars in cash withdrawals from Saudi embassy-related accounts and led to a July 2003 cease-and-desist order. In May 2004 FinCEN and the OCC assessed a concurrent $25 million civil money penalty for Bank Secrecy Act violations. A July 2004 Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations report found Riggs had helped Pinochet conceal assets. On January 27, 2005 Riggs pleaded guilty to a Bank Secrecy Act violation and agreed to a $16 million fine. PNC Financial Services Group acquired Riggs effective May 13, 2005.

facts.claim: The OCC began a targeted examination of Riggs' embassy banking business, particularly the Saudi embassy accounts, in January 2003; it lasted about five months and found serious Bank Secrecy Act compliance deficiencies that resulted in the bank's failure to identify and report suspicious transactions in the Saudi embassy accounts. Those findings formed the basis for the OCC's July 16, 2003 cease-and-desist (consent) order.
facts.quote: The examination we began in January of 2003 focused on Riggs' embassy banking business and, in particular, on the Saudi accounts.

sources.title: Testimony of Daniel P. Stipano before the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations
Cease and Desist Order 2003-79, Riggs Bank N.A.

facts.claim: The OCC's 2004 enforcement action stated that Riggs failed to identify or monitor suspicious activity including tens of millions of dollars in cash withdrawals from accounts related to the Saudi Arabian embassy, dozens of sequentially numbered international drafts totaling millions of dollars, and dozens of sequentially numbered cashier's checks. The OCC said it cooperated extensively with law enforcement investigations into certain suspicious transactions involving the Saudi embassy relationship.
facts.quote: (a) tens of millions of dollars in cash withdrawals from accounts related to the Saudi Arabian embassy; (b) dozens of sequentially-numbered international drafts that totaled millions of dollars

sources.title: Civil Money Penalty Order 2004-44, Riggs Bank N.A.
Testimony of Daniel P. Stipano before the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations

facts.claim: On May 13, 2004, FinCEN assessed a $25 million civil money penalty against Riggs Bank N.A., then the largest ever under the Bank Secrecy Act, finding that Riggs willfully failed to establish an adequate anti-money laundering program, to file timely and complete suspicious activity reports, and to file accurate currency transaction reports. The penalty was concurrent with a $25 million OCC penalty, satisfied by a single $25 million payment to the Treasury; Riggs consented without admitting or denying the findings.
facts.quote: This penalty assessment shall be concurrent with the $25 million penalty assessed against Riggs by the OCC. The penalty assessment of FinCEN and the OCC referenced above shall be satisfied by one payment of $25 million to the Department of the Treasury.

facts.claim: The Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations' July 14, 2004 minority staff report used Riggs as a case study of Patriot Act enforcement and examined the Pinochet and Equatorial Guinea accounts. It stated that Riggs' two largest embassy clients were Equatorial Guinea and Saudi Arabia, and that it did not present information about the Saudi accounts because the full Governmental Affairs Committee, under Chairman Susan Collins, was separately investigating them.
facts.quote: Because this review is ongoing under the direction of Committee Chairman Susan Collins, this Report does not present information about the Saudi accounts.

facts.claim: The July 2004 Senate subcommittee report found that Riggs Bank assisted Augusto Pinochet, former president of Chile, to evade legal proceedings related to his Riggs accounts, resisted OCC oversight of those accounts, and concealed their existence from OCC examiners for two years. Senator Levin said Riggs opened a personal account for Pinochet and helped him set up two Bahamas shell corporations, Ashburton and Althorp; the report said Pinochet deposited between $4 million and $8 million at Riggs from 1994 to 2002.
facts.quote: Riggs Bank assisted Augusto Pinochet, former president of Chile, to evade legal proceedings related to his Riggs bank accounts and resisted OCC oversight of these accounts.

facts.claim: A later Levin-Coleman staff report (2005) found the Riggs-Pinochet relationship was more extensive than previously disclosed, encompassing 28 accounts instead of nine and spanning 25 years instead of eight, and identified other institutions that held Pinochet-related funds, including Citigroup, Banco de Chile-United States and Espirito Santo Bank in Miami.
facts.quote: the relationship between Riggs Bank and Augusto Pinochet was more extensive than previously disclosed, encompassing 28 accounts instead of nine, spanning 25 years instead of eight

facts.claim: At the July 15, 2004 Senate hearing, OCC Deputy Chief Counsel Daniel Stipano acknowledged that the OCC should have been more aggressive in insisting on remedial steps earlier and should have done more extensive probing and transaction testing of the embassy accounts, noting that OCC procedures called for transactional reviews of high-risk accounts but that until 2003 this was not done at Riggs for the Saudi embassy and Equatorial Guinea accounts.
facts.quote: We should have been more aggressive in our insistence on remedial steps at an earlier time. We also should have done more extensive probing and transaction testing of the Embassy accounts.

sources.title: Testimony of Daniel P. Stipano before the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations

facts.claim: The Washington Post reported on April 7, 2004 that the FBI was investigating banking transactions by Saudi officials at Riggs, including millions of dollars in deposits and withdrawals made the previous December by Saudi ambassador Prince Bandar bin Sultan; when a representative of the ambassador declined to explain them, Riggs reported the activity as suspicious to the Treasury Department, which led the bank to end its relationship with the Saudi embassy.
facts.quote: including millions of dollars in deposits and withdrawals made in December by the Saudi ambassador, Prince Bandar bin Sultan

sources.title: Saudi Money at Riggs Probed

facts.claim: Newsweek reported, citing government documents, that a federal probe of the Saudi embassy's Riggs accounts flagged more than $27 million in transactions as suspicious, including payments to Muslim charities, clerics and Saudi students under scrutiny, and that in November 2003 Riggs filed a suspicious activity report disclosing that over four months $17.4 million from the Saudi Defense Ministry account had been disbursed to a single individual in Saudi Arabia described as coordinating construction for Prince Bandar. U.S. officials said they had identified no evidence of knowing Saudi aid to terrorist groups.
facts.quote: In November 2003, Riggs filed a "suspicious activity report" with the Treasury Department disclosing that over a four-month period, $17.4 million from the Saudi Defense account had been disbursed to a single individual in Saudi Arabia.

sources.title: Exclusive: New Questions About Saudi Money, and Bandar
Bandar and the $2 Billion Question

facts.claim: The declassified 28 pages of the 2002 Joint Inquiry state that in a search of Osama Bassnan's residence the FBI found copies of 31 cashier's checks totaling $74,000, dated February 22, 1999 to May 30, 2002, payable to Bassnan's wife and drawn on the Riggs Bank account of Prince Bandar's wife, ostensibly for nursing services; the FBI determined that at least some of these checks were given to the wife of Omar al-Bayoumi. The 9/11 Commission later found no evidence that Princess Haifa al Faisal provided funds to the conspiracy, directly or indirectly.
facts.quote: In a recent search of Bassnan's residence, the FBI located copies of 31 cashier's checks totaling $74,000, during the period February 22, 1999 to May 30, 2002. These checks were payable to Bassnan's wife and were drawn on the Riggs Bank account of Prince Bandar's wife.

facts.claim: On January 27, 2005, Riggs Bank pleaded guilty in federal court in Washington to a criminal violation of the Bank Secrecy Act for repeated and systemic failure to accurately report suspicious transactions in accounts owned and controlled by Augusto Pinochet and the government of Equatorial Guinea, agreeing to a $16 million fine and five years of corporate probation, which prosecutors called the largest criminal fine ever imposed on a bank of its size. The plea was entered before Judge Ricardo M. Urbina.
facts.quote: When sentenced by United States District Judge Ricardo M. Urbina later this Spring, Riggs will be fined $16 million and placed on a five-year period of corporate probation.

facts.claim: U.S. Attorney Kenneth Wainstein said at the plea: 'Despite numerous warnings from regulators, Riggs courted customers who were a high risk for money laundering and helped them shield their financial transactions from scrutiny.'
facts.quote: Despite numerous warnings from regulators, Riggs courted customers who were a high risk for money laundering and helped them shield their financial transactions from scrutiny.

facts.claim: PNC Financial Services Group and Riggs National Corporation signed an amended and restated merger agreement on February 10, 2005 at $20 per share, about $652 million, down from the $779 million deal announced in July 2004; PNC Bank N.A. took over the assets of Riggs Bank N.A. The OCC approved the combination on April 25, 2005, and PNC completed the acquisition effective May 13, 2005.
facts.quote: PNC completed the deal effective May 13, 2005.

connections.claim: Prince Bandar bin Sultan, as Saudi ambassador, held and had signature authority over accounts at Riggs; the Washington Post reported in April 2004 that the FBI was examining millions of dollars of his December 2003 deposits and withdrawals, and Riggs filed a suspicious activity report and ended the Saudi embassy relationship. Bandar has said the accounts were official Saudi Ministry of Defense and Aviation accounts, not personal ones.
connections.quote: including millions of dollars in deposits and withdrawals made in December by the Saudi ambassador, Prince Bandar bin Sultan

connections.claim: The Saudi Arabian embassy was one of Riggs' two largest embassy banking clients, with more than 150 associated accounts according to the Senate subcommittee; the OCC found tens of millions of dollars in cash withdrawals from Saudi embassy-related accounts that Riggs failed to report, and Riggs ended the relationship in early 2004. A Saudi spokesman denied that any embassy funds were used to support terrorism.
connections.quote: Riggs' two largest Embassy clients were Equatorial Guinea and Saudi Arabia.

openQuestions: The site's node describes Riggs accounts 'wiring funds to facilitators'. The record found shows (a) cashier's checks from Princess Haifa's Riggs account to Osama Bassnan's wife, some of which the FBI said reached Omar al-Bayoumi's wife (28 pages), and (b) a $15,000 check from Bandar cashed by Bassnan in May 1998. No official source found describes wires from Riggs to al-Bayoumi or to the hijackers, and the 9/11 Commission found no evidence that Haifa's funds reached the conspiracy.

The Senate full committee's (Collins) review of the Saudi accounts, referenced in the July 2004 PSI report, was not found as a published report; the Saudi-account detail here comes from the OCC's 2004 order and testimony, the Washington Post and Newsweek. The task's '$17M+ cash withdrawals' figure was not found; the closest figures are the OCC's 'tens of millions of dollars in cash withdrawals', Newsweek's $27 million in flagged transactions and $17.4 million in wire transfers from the Saudi Defense Ministry account, and a Wilson Center piece citing $36 million in withdrawals from Haifa's accounts in 2001-2002 (not recorded here as it was not verified against a primary source).

The OCC's 2004 order and testimony do not name Prince Bandar; the Bandar-specific transactions are reported by the Washington Post, Newsweek and (quoting a New York Times profile) PBS Frontline. The Frontline readings page says the OCC found Riggs should have filed SARs on more than two dozen transactions by Bandar; that passage was not verified against the OCC document.

The DOJ press release URL for the January 2005 plea sits under a justice.gov tax-division archive path as returned by search; the owner should confirm it is the D.C. U.S. Attorney's release. The final sentencing (court acceptance of the $16 million fine in March 2005) rests on a FindLaw commentary and was not recorded.
The 28 pages are cited through 28pages.org's hosted PDF and transcription plus CNN; the official copy on intelligence.house.gov was not returned by search.
